title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is vast and full of stars, why isn't every direction of the night sky ablaze with light?
summary: How a simple observation, that the night sky is dark, turns out to be evidence that the universe has a finite age, an expanding history, and a glowing birth we can still see in microwaves.
content:
Go outside on a clear, moonless night far from city lights and you will see a sky that is mostly black. This seems like the least surprising fact in the world. Yet in the nineteenth century the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers sharpened a puzzle that had nagged Kepler and Halley before him: if the universe is infinite, eternal, and evenly filled with stars, the night sky should not be dark at all. It should blaze, in every direction, as brightly as the surface of the Sun.

The Argument

Imagine the sky divided into thin concentric shells centered on Earth. A distant shell's stars each look dimmer, falling off with the square of distance. But a distant shell is also larger, and its area grows with the square of distance too, so it contains proportionally more stars. The two effects cancel exactly: every shell contributes the same amount of light. Add up infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness, or, once nearer stars block farther ones, a sky where every line of sight ends on a stellar surface. Look anywhere and you are looking at a star.

The dark sky is therefore not a trivial observation. It is evidence. Something in the assumptions (infinite, eternal, static, uniform) must be wrong.

Failed Escapes

Olbers himself proposed that interstellar dust absorbs the distant light. This fails on thermodynamic grounds: in an eternal universe the dust would absorb energy until it heated up and glowed as brightly as the stars. Others suggested a hierarchical, fractal arrangement of stars that thins out with scale, an idea that has occasionally resurfaced but does not match how galaxies are actually distributed on the largest scales.

The Real Answer: A Universe With a History

The resolution is that the universe is not eternal in the needed sense. Light travels at a finite speed and the cosmos has a finite age, about 13.8 billion years. We can only see light that has had time to reach us, so our view is bounded by a horizon. Within that observable volume there are simply not enough stars to fill every line of sight. Remarkably, the first person to state this answer clearly was not a physicist but Edgar Allan Poe, in his 1848 prose poem Eureka.

Stars also have finite lifetimes. Even an infinitely old universe could not keep them shining forever; there is not enough fuel to light the sky to stellar-surface brightness. Lord Kelvin worked this out quantitatively in 1901.

Expansion adds a second effect. Light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer wavelengths, which drains its energy. Most cosmologists consider the finite age the dominant reason and redshift a supporting one.

The Sky Is Not Actually Dark

Here is the twist. Look in every direction with microwave eyes and the sky does glow, almost perfectly uniformly. This is the cosmic microwave background: light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old and as hot as the surface of a star. In that sense Olbers was right. Every line of sight does end on a glowing surface, the surface of last scattering. Expansion has simply stretched that glow by a factor of about 1,100, from visible orange to invisible microwaves at 2.7 kelvin.

So the darkness of night is a message written across the whole sky: the universe had a beginning, it has been expanding, and we live in an era late enough that its fiery origin has cooled into a faint hum.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite age of the universe and the speed of light create an observable horizon. Darkness is a direct consequence of the Big Bang model, not a neutral backdrop.

perspectives.title: Thermodynamics Perspective
perspectives.description: Absorbing dust cannot hide starlight forever: in equilibrium it would glow too. And stars have finite fuel, so an eternally bright sky would violate energy conservation.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Kepler, Halley, Cheseaux, and Olbers all wrestled with the problem, and Poe guessed the answer decades before physics could confirm it. The paradox shows how everyday facts can hold deep clues.

perspectives.title: Philosophy Perspective
perspectives.description: Olbers' paradox is a model case of reasoning from absence. What we fail to see can constrain reality as strongly as what we do see.

connections: Cosmological redshift and the expanding universe
The observable universe and cosmic horizons
openQuestions: How should we weigh the finite age of the universe against redshift when explaining the darkness, and does the answer depend on the cosmological model?
If the universe's expansion keeps accelerating, how dark will the sky become for observers trillions of years from now?
Are there other everyday observations that quietly encode deep facts about cosmology?
What would astronomy and philosophy have looked like on a planet where the night sky was not dark?
